title: A crowd copies its way wrong
hook: 100 people see each other's picks. Do their separate clues still add up?

knows: a clue right 2 times in 3 beats a coin flip
doesNotKnow: that a pick copied from a crowd is not an independent clue
that a crowd can stop adding information after two matching picks

misconception: When many people independently choose the same way, they are probably right.
objective: The learner can say that in the urn model a crowd locks onto the wrong colour about 1 time in 5 (clue right 2 in 3), because after a lead of 2 nobody's own clue changes the pick, while a plain vote of the same clues is wrong about 1 time in 5,000.
keyState: At least 100 crowds run (the Run 100 chip) and the pooled view opened. On the QA click path (Run 1, Run 100, Run 10,000) that is 10,101 crowds at clue right 2 in 3: 2,009 wrong (19.9%), pooled vote wrong in 2.

claims.text: The urn is blue. Everyone sees the earlier picks; a person who sees one colour lead by 2 or more copies it, and otherwise (a lead of 0 or 1, ties included) follows their own clue.
claims.source: model.ts sequence(): lead = blue picks minus red picks so far; |lead| >= 2 copies the leader, else pick = own clue. The urn is blue in every run; the clue is blue with probability ACC. Rule as in Easley & Kleinberg 2010 ch. 16 (section unconfirmed; tie rule chosen here and disclosed).

claims.text: Once one colour leads the picks by 2, every later person (clue right 2 times in 3) copies it whatever their own clue says, so the crowd adds no new information.
claims.source: Bayes' rule with equal priors: two net matching signals give posterior odds 2^2 = 4 to 1 for the leader; one opposing clue brings it to 2 to 1, still favouring the leader (a tie is broken by the own clue, per c1). Easley & Kleinberg 2010 ch. 16 (section unconfirmed; the book's urn model §16.2-16.4 from memory of the contents).

claims.text: With clues right 2 times in 3, the chance the crowd locks onto the wrong colour is 1/5 = 20%. (Shown as 'exact: 20.0%' beside the learner's tally.)
claims.source: Until the lead reaches 2 every pick equals its clue, so the lead is a gambler's-ruin walk with step +1 at probability p = 2/3 and -1 at q = 1/3, absorbed at +-2: P(red) = q^2/(q^2+p^2) = (1/9)/(5/9) = 1/5. Node check 2026-10-14: seeds 1..10,000 give 1,991 wrong (19.9%), seeds 1..101 give 18 wrong, seeds 1..10,101 give 2,009 wrong; every one of 10,000 sequences reached a lead of 2 (latest at person 27).

claims.text: If the first two clues are both wrong (a 1 in 9 chance when clues are right 2 in 3), the crowd locks onto the wrong colour.
claims.source: Two red clues give two red picks, a lead of 2, so by c2 everyone copies red. P = (1/3)^2 = 1/9. Seeds 1..10,000: 1,080 of 10,000 start with two red clues (10.8%).

claims.text: A plain vote of the same 100 clues (each right 2 times in 3) is wrong with probability about 0.0199% (about 1 in 5,000), plus 0.0220% for an exact 50-50 tie. On the stage, 'Pooled wrong' counts the runs whose 100 clues have a red majority; ties are not counted.
claims.source: Exact binomial, computed in node 2026-10-14: P(blue clues < 50) = 0.0001989, P(= 50) = 0.0002204 with 100 clues at p = 2/3. Seeds 1..10,000: 2 red majorities and 3 ties; seeds 1..10,101: 2 and 3. Reveal quotes the learner's own count of red majorities.

claims.text: With clues right 60% of the time the crowd is wrong about 30.8% of the time; with clues right 80% of the time, about 5.9% (the same formula q^2/(q^2+p^2)). The reveal quotes the exact figure for the accuracy the learner ran most.
Seed and counting rules are disclosed: crowd number k uses mulberry32(k), counted separately for each clue accuracy; 'Runs (seeds 1 to n)' shows n.
claims.source: model.ts runMore() and sequence(); Demo.tsx readout label. Seeds are not chosen: they are 1, 2, 3, ... in order.

claims.text: (Not shown to the learner; dropped.) In the classroom urn experiment of Anderson and Holt (1997) cascades formed in the lab.
claims.source: Brief planned claim 4. NEEDS A HUMAN SOURCE CHECK by the fact-checker (Anderson & Holt 1997, American Economic Review). Not used in the lesson text, so no learner sees it unverified; kept here so the check is not lost.

recall.question: 100 people each get a private clue (right 2 times in 3), see all earlier picks and choose. After two matching picks, what does a person's own clue do?
options: It no longer changes their pick, so the crowd adds no new information
recall.why: Two matching picks put the odds at 4 to 1; one opposing clue only brings them to 2 to 1, so the person copies. The crowd was wrong about 1 time in 5.

references.note: Information cascades, urn experiment; section unconfirmed (16.2-16.5 from memory of the contents)
